opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think there's a very direct connection, and it's one that people sometimes underestimate. Governments can't regulate what they can't measure. If a regulator says, "Your system must not be able to help someone build a bioweapon," or "Your system must not deceive its operators," that's only meaningful if we have scientific methods to test for those properties, ideally with some level of confidence. Right now, our ability to do that is quite limited.

So the first role of technical safety research is building the measuring instruments: evaluations, red-teaming methodologies, ways of probing for dangerous capabilities and for dangerous intentions or tendencies in the model. Without that, legislation ends up either very vague, which lets companies interpret it however they like, or it relies entirely on self-reporting by the developers, which is clearly not enough when there are such strong commercial pressures.

The second role is about what we ask companies to demonstrate. In other high-risk industries, like aviation, pharmaceuticals, or nuclear, the burden of proof is on the developer to show that the product is safe enough. I'd like to see the same thing for frontier AI. But for that, we need research that tells us what a convincing safety case even looks like. What kind of evidence would give us, say, high confidence that a system won't take catastrophic actions? Today, honestly, nobody can provide that kind of guarantee for the most capable systems. That's a gap science has to fill, and it's part of why I've been working on approaches that aim for quantitative, probabilistic guarantees, for example systems that estimate the probability that an action could cause harm and refuse when that probability is too high.

And third, research helps governments understand where we are on the trajectory. Policymakers need an honest, scientifically grounded picture of the capabilities and risks, which was the motivation behind the International AI Safety Report. If the science is clear and shared across countries, it becomes much easier to agree on requirements, and harder for anyone to say, "Well, we don't really know if this is a problem."

So I'd say technical safety research and governance are not separate tracks. Regulation sets the incentives and the obligations, but it's the science that makes those obligations concrete, verifiable, and enforceable. And I think we need a lot more public investment in that science, not just research happening inside the companies whose products are being evaluated.

r001.rationale: The response says safety research can make requirements concrete, verifiable, and enforceable, but does not say that demonstrating economically competitive, safe systems would make requirements easier to impose.

r002.rationale: The response discusses commercial pressures on developers and policymakers’ uncertainty, but does not state that governments’ focus on economic competition causes them to overlook AI risks.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the two go hand in hand, and that's actually one of the reasons I've been putting more of my own effort into the technical side in the last few years. Governments can say, "You must make sure your system is safe," but that sentence only means something if there's a way to check it. Right now, in many cases, there isn't. So the first way technical research helps is simply by making the requirement well-defined.

Think about how it works in other industries. If you regulate airplanes, or drugs, or nuclear plants, you don't just tell the companies "be careful." You have standards, you have tests, you have thresholds, and those come from decades of science and engineering. With AI, we are at the very beginning of that. We don't yet have a reliable way to look at a frontier model and say with confidence what it can do, what it cannot do, and whether it will behave as intended once it's deployed. So evaluations, red-teaming methodologies, interpretability tools, ways to bound the probability of harmful behavior... all of that is really the scientific infrastructure that regulators will need in order to write rules that can be enforced rather than rules that are just aspirational.

The second thing is that technical research can shift the burden of proof in a healthy direction. Right now, it's mostly the public, or academics, or civil society that has to show something is dangerous after the fact. What I'd like to see, and what the Safety Institutes and some of the work around the International AI Safety Report are moving toward, is that developers demonstrate safety before deployment, the way a pharmaceutical company has to show a drug is safe. But for that to be fair and workable, the methods have to exist. You can't demand a safety case if nobody knows how to build one. So part of my motivation with the work on quantitative safety guarantees, with the idea of what I've been calling a "Scientist AI," a non-agentic system that is primarily trying to understand and estimate probabilities rather than pursue goals, is to give both companies and governments something concrete they could eventually point to.

And then there's a third, more political aspect, which I think people underestimate. Governments are very hesitant to impose constraints when they're told that doing so will kill innovation or hand the lead to a competitor. Good technical safety research weakens that argument. If you can show that there are methods that make systems safer without making them useless, or that there are ways to monitor and verify compliance, including across borders, then regulators are on much firmer ground. The more credible the science, the harder it is to dismiss safety requirements as naive.

I'd add one caveat, because I don't want to sound overly optimistic. The technical work is necessary but not sufficient. There's a real danger that evaluations give a false sense of security, that a model passes some tests and everyone relaxes while the actual capabilities, or the actual risks, were somewhere the tests didn't look. So the research community also has a responsibility to be honest about uncertainty, to tell governments what we don't know, not just what we can measure. In my view, that honesty about the limits of our understanding is itself one of the most important inputs to policy, because it's what justifies caution and things like compute thresholds or pre-deployment requirements even when we can't yet point to a precise mechanism of harm.

r001.rationale: The response says technical research can show systems can be made safer without becoming useless, weakening concerns that safety rules would kill innovation or hand an advantage to competitors.

r002.rationale: It says competition concerns make governments hesitant to impose constraints, but does not state that governments overlook AI risks.

astra-6.text:
I think technical AI safety research can help governments turn a general demand — “these systems should be safe” — into requirements that can actually be tested. What kinds of dangerous capabilities should we evaluate? How do we assess whether the safeguards work? And what evidence should a company have to provide before deploying a system?

But we have to be careful about what those tests establish. If you fail to elicit a dangerous behaviour, that doesn’t mean the system is incapable of it. So part of the research is understanding the limitations of our evaluations, and developing stronger ways of providing assurance.

There’s a division of responsibility here. Scientists can help describe the risks, develop measurement tools, and explain how much confidence the evidence warrants. Governments have to decide what level of risk is acceptable and what obligations to impose. Technical research makes those decisions better informed; it doesn’t replace them.

r001.rationale: The response says technical research can make safety requirements testable and better informed, but does not state that demonstrating economically competitive, safe AI systems would make requirements easier to impose.

r002.rationale: The response does not say governments overlook AI risks because they focus on AI-driven economic competition.

sol-6.1.text:
I think technical AI safety research can help governments turn a general objective—“these systems should be safe”—into concrete requirements. What should a developer have to demonstrate before deploying a powerful system? What kinds of tests would provide meaningful evidence, and what are the limitations of those tests? Those are technical questions, even though the decision about how much risk society should accept is a political one.

One difficulty is that showing a model behaves well in a set of evaluations doesn’t establish that it will behave well in every circumstance. So research needs to help us understand what we can actually guarantee, where we’re relying on assumptions, and where we simply don’t know. Governments need that distinction to avoid requiring something that sounds reassuring but doesn’t provide much protection.

And this should be an ongoing process. As our understanding improves, the requirements should improve too. You don’t need to wait until we have solved every scientific problem before regulating, but you do need independent scientific expertise to make the regulation meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response says technical research can help turn safety objectives into concrete requirements, but it does not say that demonstrating economically competitive, safe AI systems would make requirements easier to impose.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that governments’ focus on AI-driven economic competition causes them to overlook AI risks.
